stops.name: Kerman, the desert of salt and poison springs
stops.campa: Back through Kerman, province of turquoise and steel, the Polos fill skins of goat-hide with water and turn east into the Dasht-e Lut, the desert the Persians call the Plain of Emptiness, where the springs run bitter with salt or poisoned with copper and a careless mouthful can kill a man within a day. Seven days they cross it, resting at a walled town before the ordeal to rest men and beasts, then eight days more of gravel and dead ground before green country and the first villages of Khorasan rise on the far side of the waste.

stops.name: Balkh, the ruined city of Alexander
stops.campa: The road climbs into ancient Balkh, a great and splendid city once, Marco notes, until the Tartars sacked and half-ruined it; the natives still say Alexander the Great took a wife here, a daughter of Darius, and point to broken marble as proof. Wolves and lions are said to prowl the wasted quarters by night. From Balkh the country begins visibly to climb: orchards give way to bare hills, the air thins, and the caravan turns south and east toward Badakhshan, where the mountains that will not let them down again for months on end begin in earnest.
stops.quote: Balc is a noble city and a great, though it was much greater in former days. But the Tartars and other nations have greatly ravaged and destroyed it.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XXVIII (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Badakhshan, the mountains of ruby and healthful air
stops.campa: Badakhshan yields the finest rubies in the world, mined by the king's own license from a mountain called Syghinan on pain of death for any who dig without leave, and lapis lazuli besides, ground to the blue of heaven for painters' pigment. The mountain air, Marco writes with a traveler's relief, is so wholesome that a man sick in the plains climbs two days into these heights and is cured, sound within three days more, a note he sets down, some readers guess, from his own convalescence here after the fevers of the long lowland roads behind him.
stops.quote: It is in this province that those fine and valuable gems the Balas Rubies are found... There is also in the same country another mountain, in which azure is found; 'tis the finest in the world.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XXIX (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: The Pamir, forty days on the roof of the world
stops.campa: Twelve days up a river gorge and then onto the Pamir itself, a plain the natives call Bam-i-Dunya, the Roof of the World, where no bird flies for the thinness of the air and no fire burns bright or cooks food well at such height, and the cold is bitter even at high summer. Twelve days more of this desolate tableland, without house or habitation, before the road descends at last toward Kashgar, the hardest single stretch of the whole outward road, by Marco's own account, and the gate into the Tartar-held towns of the true Silk Road.
stops.quote: The plain is called Pamier, and you ride across it for twelve days together, finding nothing but a desert without habitations or any green thing, so that travellers are obliged to carry with them whatever they have need of.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XXXII (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Kashgar
stops.campa: Kashgar sits fat and fertile after the Pamir's hunger, its orchards of cotton, flax, and vine watering the caravans before the last, worst desert. Nestorian Christians keep their own churches here beside the mosques, a reminder that the road to Cathay is not only a Tartar road but a Christian one too, laid down by merchants and monks centuries before the Polos rode it. Marco lingers over the local reputation for sharp dealing and usury he lays on the Kashgaris, the merchant's habitual eye for who can be trusted on the next long stage of the road ahead.

stops.name: Yarkand
stops.campa: Yarkand offers little the canon dwells on save its people's poor eyesight, which Marco blames on the water and the diet, and the goitres common in the throats of those who drink it, one of the small clinical asides that fill his book between princes and marvels. The caravan rests and resupplies for the harder ground ahead: Khotan's jade rivers first, then the true desert, the Lop, where the road narrows to single file between dunes that swallow whole parties who wander from the line of footprints and bleached bone marking the only safe way through.

stops.name: Khotan, the jade rivers
stops.campa: Khotan's two rivers run down from the mountains carrying jade in their gravel beds, white and green stone that Chinese buyers prize above gold and that local diggers wade the shallows by moonlight to gather before the current shifts it downstream. The province is rich in cotton, grain, and vineyards, its people already subject to the Great Khan, a full eight days short of the true wilderness. Beyond Khotan the settled world gives out; the road threads a chain of small oasis-towns and then simply stops at the ragged edge of the Desert of Lop.

stops.name: The Desert of Lop, voices of spirits in the sands
stops.campa: A month across the Desert of Lop, water found only at rare and bitter wells, and Marco records what the guides swear is true: a straggler behind his company, riding by night, will hear his own name called and the tramp of a following troop, and following the voice will be led from the road and never found again; and that not by night alone but even at noon the air fills with drums and clashing arms and many instruments, though no living thing stands in sight for a hundred miles. Travelers hang bells on their beasts and mark cairns to hold the line.
stops.quote: Even in the day-time one hears those spirits talking. And sometimes you shall hear the sound of a variety of musical instruments, and still more commonly the sound of drums.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XXXIX (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Ganzhou, a year among the idol-worshippers
stops.campa: Out of the Lop into Tangut country and the city of Ganzhou, the Polos halt a full year: trade, Marco says plainly, kept them, though the delay also lets Nicolò and Maffeo mend their fortune before the last leg to court. Here for the first time the travelers meet in numbers the Buddhist and Nestorian communities of the Tartar borderlands side by side, temples of gilded idols and Christian crosses within a bowshot of each other, the first hint of the vast religious tolerance Marco will find astonishing at Kublai's own court further east.

stops.name: Shangdu (Xanadu), arrival at the summer court of Kublai Khan
stops.campa: Three and a half years from Acre, the Polos ride into Shangdu, Kublai's summer capital, where a marble palace gilt and painted with beasts and birds stands inside a walled park of fountains and grazing deer, and beside it a whole pavilion of gilded and lacquered cane that can be taken down, cane and cord and all, and carried wherever the Emperor commands. Nicolò presents the golden tablet and the oil of the Sepulchre; Kublai receives them, and the young Marco, twenty-one now, kneels with his father and uncle, unaware he has just entered the seventeen years that will make his name outlast every court here.
stops.quote: There is at this place a very fine marble Palace, the rooms of which are all gilt and painted with figures of men and beasts and birds... inside the Park there are fountains and rivers and brooks, and beautiful meadows, with all kinds of wild animals.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. LXI (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Khanbaliq, taken into the Khan's own service
stops.campa: At the winter capital of Khanbaliq, Kublai finds in the young Venetian a gift for languages and a merchant's eye for the odd fact that pleases him more than any formal report, and takes Marco into personal service, sending him on missions through the provinces of Cathay and Manzi that other envoys narrate dryly and that Marco returns from full of tales of custom, marvel, and revenue, exactly what the Khan wants of him. He learns Mongol and at least one Chinese dialect, some sources claim four tongues in all, and rises within a few years to posts of genuine trust.

stops.name: Khanbaliq: the bark of trees that passes for money, the post-roads
stops.campa: Two wonders of Kublai's rule strike Marco harder than any temple: paper money, stamped with the Khan's own seal from the inner bark of the mulberry and passed current through the length of the empire as though it were gold, refused by no man on pain of death; and the post-roads, three hundred paces wide, planted with shade trees, strung every twenty-five miles with a post-house of four hundred horses, so that a courier belted with warning bells can cover two hundred and fifty miles between one sunrise and the next across the whole breadth of Cathay.
stops.quote: All these pieces of paper are issued with as much solemnity and authority as if they were of pure gold or silver... and indeed everybody takes them readily, for wheresoever a person may go throughout the Great Kaan's dominions he shall find these pieces of paper current.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, ch. XXIV (Yule-Cordier translation)
